text: How do you dig a subway tunnel without tearing up the city? You send in a tunnel boring machine.
Think of it as a factory on rails: a giant drill up front, and a moving construction site behind it.
The cutterhead spins a few times a minute. Steel disc cutters press into the rock until it cracks and chips away.
In soft ground, pressurized soil or slurry holds up the face, so the earth doesn't collapse.
Behind the cutterhead, a steel shield keeps the tunnel open while the crew works inside.
The broken rock, called muck, is scooped up, carried back by a screw conveyor, then belted out of the tunnel.
Now the clever part. A robotic arm sets curved concrete segments into a ring, building the tunnel lining as it goes.
Hydraulic rams push off that fresh ring to shove the whole machine forward. Adjust the rams, and it steers.
Cut, muck, ring, push. Repeat, around the clock.
New York's Second Avenue Subway machine was four hundred fifty feet long, and averaged about sixty feet a day under Manhattan.
Congrats! You've discovered the tunnel boring machine.
